entry.title: Cheap runners for most CI jobs, fast runners for the few that matter
entry.summary:
We build Sengi, a hosted runner service for GitHub Actions. Today we launched Sengi Basic, at $1 per 1,000 runner minutes. This post is about the idea behind it: pick the runner per job, not per company. Look at a typical workflow run. Lint, unit tests, type checks, dependency audits, nightly jobs. Nobody is waiting on most of them. Then there are one or two jobs everyone is waiting on: the Docker image, the release build, the slow integration suite blocking a merge. Paying the same per-minute rate for both makes no sense. So Sengi has two classes:
Size Basic Premium GitHub-hosted Linux
2 vCPU $0.001/min $0.003/min $0.006/min
4 vCPU $0.002/min $0.006/min $0.012/min
8 vCPU $0.004/min $0.012/min $0.022/min
Basic gives you six times the minutes per dollar of GitHub's own runners at 2 and 4 vCPU, and 5.5 times at 8 vCPU. 10,000 2-vCPU minutes cost $10 on Basic and $60 on GitHub at list price. Premium is the fast class. On a PostHog Docker build at 4 vCPU it finished in 7m34s; GitHub's runner took 14m36s. The class is just the label: jobs: lint: runs-on: sengi-basic-2-ubuntu-2404 steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v4 - run: npm ci && npm run lint
test: runs-on: sengi-basic-4-ubuntu-2404 steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v4 - run: npm ci && npm test
image: needs: test runs-on: sengi-premium-8-ubuntu-2404 steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v4 - run: docker build -t app .
Labels: sengi-basic-{2,4,8}-ubuntu-2404 and sengi-premium-{2,4,8}-ubuntu-2404. Workflows, secrets and logs stay in GitHub Actions. Move every job to Basic. Find the jobs where someone is waiting on the result. Run those on Premium and compare time and cost against Basic. Keep whichever wins for that job. Every account gets 3,000 free Basic minutes a month. A 4-vCPU minute counts as two and an 8-vCPU minute as four. More on Basic vs Premium: https://sengi.run/blog/sengi-basic-vs-premium

entry.title: Sprint Capacity Planning in Azure DevOps: Handling Public Holidays, PTO, and Story-Level Rollups
entry.summary: A recurring question on Stack Overflow and Manual Holiday Math: Distributed engineering teams have different national and regional public holidays. Manually subtracting days off per developer every sprint is error-prone. Disconnected Time Logs & Capacity Bars: Capacity bars only work if Remaining Work and Completed Work stay synchronized as tasks move from Active to Resolved. Cross-Project Blind Spots: Engineers shared across two repositories or project spaces appear at 100% capacity in both unless hours roll up centrally. In VelocyTrack, we unified sprint capacity planning directly with the daily engineering backlog: Automated Regional Holiday & Absence Deduction: Assign a country/state calendar per team member and record PTO once - available sprint hours recalculate automatically. Real-Time Commitment vs. Capacity Gauge: See immediately whether a sprint is under-allocated, balanced, or over-committed across all 4 Azure DevOps process templates (Scrum, Agile, Basic, CMMI). Zero Source Code Storage: Operates strictly on work item and Git metadata via AES-256 encrypted tokens. You can explore a seeded sprint capacity & timelog workspace directly in your browser without signing up: Explore the Live VelocyTrack Sandbox

entry.title: How Does a Live Wallpaper Draw Behind Your Desktop Icons on Windows?
entry.summary: Live wallpaper apps like EWRE play a video behind your desktop icons, but in front of the static wallpaper. Windows has no public API for that. So how is it done? This post explains the well-known technique that wallpaper engines use. It relies on undocumented shell behavior, so treat it as a field guide rather than a contract. Your desktop is a stack of ordinary windows owned by Explorer: Progman: the Program Manager window, the root of the desktop. SHELLDLL_DefView: the window that draws your icons. WorkerW: a helper window. The static wallpaper is painted into one of these. The goal is to place your own window behind the icons (SHELLDLL_DefView) and in front of the static wallpaper. Sending Progman an undocumented message, 0x052C, makes it spawn a WorkerW window sitting behind the icon …
